methodology: QA-only architecture comparison on the exact reliability run confirmed memories, facets, revisions and original sources. No new extraction or formal-memory writes. Actual production retrieval may include typed full source passages; retention judges still see formal memory content only. Both QA entries run now, and their answers are anonymously regraded against historical reliability answers. Human gold enters only the unchanged isolated post-hoc judges. Same-model judging is not independent human validation.

documents.title: Contextualize, Show and Tell: A Neural Visual Storyteller

questions.question: Is the position in the sequence part of the input?

result.answer:
是。模型为图像序列的每个位置设置一个独立解码器，每个解码器以对应图像的嵌入 e(I_i) 作为第一项输入，因此序列中的位置对应各自的输入图像。 [1][2][3]
每个解码器针对序列中对应位置学习特定的语言模型，例如第一个解码器学习故事开头句、最后一个解码器学习结尾句。 [4][5]

citations.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p1]] Our model contains five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence. All the 5 decoders use the last hidden state of the encoder (i.e. the context) as its first hidden state and take the corresponding image embedding as its first input. In this way, the first decoder generates the sequence of words for the first image in the sequence, the second decoder for the second image in the sequence, and so on. This allows each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence. For instance, the first decoder will learn the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder the closing sentences. The word embeddings were computed using word2vec BIBREF8 .

memories.content: Having an independent decoder for each position of the image sequence, allowed our visual storyteller to build more specific language models using the context vector as its first state and the image embedding as its first input.

evidence.sourceTitle: Contextualize, Show and Tell: A Neural Visual Storyteller
evidence.text: p0]] Our visual storyteller incorporates a context encoder and multiple independent decoders to the image description architecture by BIBREF0 to generate stories from image sequences. Having an independent decoder for each position of the image sequence, allowed our visual storyteller to build more specific language models using the context vector as its first state and the image embedding as its first input. In the internal track of the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018, we obtained competitive METEOR scores in both the public and hidden test sets and performed well in the human evaluation.

evidence.text: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s3:p0]] The model's first component is a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), more precisely an LSTM that summarizes the sequence of images. At every timestep $t$ the network takes as input an image $I_i$ where $i\in \lbrace 1,2,3,4,5\rbrace $ from the sequence. The representation of the images was obtained through Inception V3.

evidence.sourceTitle: Contextualize, Show and Tell: A Neural Visual Storyteller
evidence.text: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s1:p1]] The visual storytelling task and dataset were introduced by BIBREF4 . This was the first dataset specifically created for visual storytelling. They proposed a baseline approach which consists of a sequence to sequence model, where the encoder takes the sequence of images as input and the decoder takes the last state of the encoder as its first state to generate the story. Since this model produces stories with generic phrases, they used decode-time heuristics to improve the generated stories.

evidence.sourceTitle: Contextualize, Show and Tell: A Neural Visual Storyteller
evidence.text: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p0]] The decoder is the second LSTM network that uses the information obtained from the encoder to generate the sequence's story. The first input $x_0$ to the decoder is the image for which the text is being generated. The last hidden state from the encoder $h_e^{(t)}$ is used to initialize the first hidden state of the decoder $h_d^{(0)}$ . With this strategy, we provide the decoder with the context of the whole sequence and the content of the current image (i.e. global and local information) to generate the corresponding text that will contribute to the overall story.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s7:p0]] Our visual storyteller incorporates a context encoder and multiple independent decoders to the image description architecture by BIBREF0 to generate stories from image sequences. Having an independent decoder for each position of the image sequence, allowed our visual storyteller to build more specific language models using the context vector as its first state and the image embedding as its first input. In the internal track of the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018, we obtained competitive METEOR scores in both the public and hidden test sets and performed well in the human evaluation.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p1]] Our model contains five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence. All the 5 decoders use the last hidden state of the encoder (i.e. the context) as its first hidden state and take the corresponding image embedding as its first input. In this way, the first decoder generates the sequence of words for the first image in the sequence, the second decoder for the second image in the sequence, and so on. This allows each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence. For instance, the first decoder will learn the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder the closing sentences. The word embeddings were computed using word2vec BIBREF8 .

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p0]] The decoder is the second LSTM network that uses the information obtained from the encoder to generate the sequence's story. The first input $x_0$ to the decoder is the image for which the text is being generated. The last hidden state from the encoder $h_e^{(t)}$ is used to initialize the first hidden state of the decoder $h_d^{(0)}$ . With this strategy, we provide the decoder with the context of the whole sequence and the content of the current image (i.e. global and local information) to generate the corresponding text that will contribute to the overall story.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p2]] Our proposed architecture is presented in Figure 3 . For each image in the sequence, we obtain its representation $\lbrace e(I_1),...,e(I_5)\rbrace $ using Inception v3. The encoder takes the images in order, one at every timestep $t$ . At time $t=5$ , we obtain the context vector through $h_e^{(t)}$ (represented by $\mathbf {Z}$ ). This vector is used to initialize each decoder's hidden state while the first input to each decoder is its corresponding image embedding $e(I_i)$ . Each decoder generates a sequence of words $\lbrace p_1,...,p_{n}\rbrace $ for each image in the sequence. The final story is the concatenation of the output of the 5 decoders.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s0:p0]] Over the past few years, generating text from images and videos has gained a lot of attention in the Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing communities and several related tasks have been proposed, such as image labeling, image and video description and visual question answering. In particular, prominent results have been achieved in image description with various deep neural network architectures, e.g. BIBREF1 , BIBREF2 , BIBREF3 , BIBREF0 . However, the need of generating more narrative texts from images which may reflect experiences, rather than just listing objects and their attributes, has given rise to tasks such as visual storytelling BIBREF4 . This task is about generating a story from a sequence of images. Figure 1 shows the difference between descriptions of images in isolation and stories for images in sequence.

references.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s7:p0]] Our visual storyteller incorporates a context encoder and multiple independent decoders to the image description architecture by BIBREF0 to generate stories from image sequences. Having an independent decoder for each position of the image sequence, allowed our visual storyteller to build more specific language models using the context vector as its first state and the image embedding as its first input. In the internal track of the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018, we obtained competitive METEOR scores in both the public and hidden test sets and performed well in the human evaluation.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p1]] Our model contains five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence. All the 5 decoders use the last hidden state of the encoder (i.e. the context) as its first hidden state and take the corresponding image embedding as its first input. In this way, the first decoder generates the sequence of words for the first image in the sequence, the second decoder for the second image in the sequence, and so on. This allows each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence. For instance, the first decoder will learn the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder the closing sentences. The word embeddings were computed using word2vec BIBREF8 .

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s3:p0]] The model's first component is a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), more precisely an LSTM that summarizes the sequence of images. At every timestep $t$ the network takes as input an image $I_i$ where $i\in \lbrace 1,2,3,4,5\rbrace $ from the sequence. At time $t=5$ , the LSTM has encoded the 5 images and provides the sequence's context through its last hidden state denoted by $h_e^{(t)}$ . The representation of the images was obtained through Inception V3.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s1:p1]] The visual storytelling task and dataset were introduced by BIBREF4 . This was the first dataset specifically created for visual storytelling. They proposed a baseline approach which consists of a sequence to sequence model, where the encoder takes the sequence of images as input and the decoder takes the last state of the encoder as its first state to generate the story. Since this model produces stories with generic phrases, they used decode-time heuristics to improve the generated stories.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p0]] The decoder is the second LSTM network that uses the information obtained from the encoder to generate the sequence's story. The first input $x_0$ to the decoder is the image for which the text is being generated. The last hidden state from the encoder $h_e^{(t)}$ is used to initialize the first hidden state of the decoder $h_d^{(0)}$ . With this strategy, we provide the decoder with the context of the whole sequence and the content of the current image (i.e. global and local information) to generate the corresponding text that will contribute to the overall story.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p2]] Our proposed architecture is presented in Figure 3 . For each image in the sequence, we obtain its representation $\lbrace e(I_1),...,e(I_5)\rbrace $ using Inception v3. The encoder takes the images in order, one at every timestep $t$ . At time $t=5$ , we obtain the context vector through $h_e^{(t)}$ (represented by $\mathbf {Z}$ ). This vector is used to initialize each decoder's hidden state while the first input to each decoder is its corresponding image embedding $e(I_i)$ . Each decoder generates a sequence of words $\lbrace p_1,...,p_{n}\rbrace $ for each image in the sequence. The final story is the concatenation of the output of the 5 decoders.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s5:p0]] The generated stories were evaluated using both automatic metrics and human ratings. The automatic evaluation was performed by computing the METEOR metric BIBREF5 on a public test set and a hidden test set. The former is a set of $1,938$ image sequences and stories taken from the test set of the VIST dataset BIBREF4 . The latter consists of new stories generated by humans from a subset of image sequences of the public test set.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s0:p0]] Over the past few years, generating text from images and videos has gained a lot of attention in the Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing communities and several related tasks have been proposed, such as image labeling, image and video description and visual question answering. In particular, prominent results have been achieved in image description with various deep neural network architectures, e.g. BIBREF1 , BIBREF2 , BIBREF3 , BIBREF0 . However, the need of generating more narrative texts from images which may reflect experiences, rather than just listing objects and their attributes, has given rise to tasks such as visual storytelling BIBREF4 . This task is about generating a story from a sequence of images. Figure 1 shows the difference between descriptions of images in isolation and stories for images in sequence.

For each image in the sequence, we obtain its representation $\lbrace e(I_1),...,e(I_5)\rbrace $ using Inception v3. The encoder takes the images in order, one at every timestep $t$ . At time $t=5$ , we obtain the context vector through $h_e^{(t)}$ (represented by $\mathbf {Z}$ ). This vector is used to initialize each decoder's hidden state while the first input to each decoder is its corresponding image embedding $e(I_i)$ . Each decoder generates a sequence of words $\lbrace p_1,...,p_{n}\rbrace $ for each image in the sequence. The final story is the concatenation of the output of the 5 decoders.

evidence.text: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s7:p0]] Our visual storyteller incorporates a context encoder and multiple independent decoders to the image description architecture by BIBREF0 to generate stories from image sequences. Having an independent decoder for each position of the image sequence, allowed our visual storyteller to build more specific language models using the context vector as its first state and the image embedding as its first input. In the internal track of the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018, we obtained competitive METEOR scores in both the public and hidden test sets and performed well in the human evaluation.

evidence.text: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p1]] Our model contains five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence. All the 5 decoders use the last hidden state of the encoder (i.e. the context) as its first hidden state and take the corresponding image embedding as its first input. In this way, the first decoder generates the sequence of words for the first image in the sequence, the second decoder for the second image in the sequence, and so on. evidence.text: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s1:p1]] The visual storytelling task and dataset were introduced by BIBREF4 . This was the first dataset specifically created for visual storytelling. They proposed a baseline approach which consists of a sequence to sequence model, where the encoder takes the sequence of images as input and the decoder takes the last state of the encoder as its first state to generate the story. The last hidden state from the encoder $h_e^{(t)}$ is used to initialize the first hidden state of the decoder $h_d^{(0)}$ . At every timestep $t$ the network takes as input an image $I_i$ where $i\in \lbrace 1,2,3,4,5\rbrace $ from the sequence. At time $t=5$ , the LSTM has encoded the 5 images and provides the sequence's context through its last hidden state denoted by $h_e^{(t)}$ . The representation of the images was obtained through Inception V3.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s1:p1]] The visual storytelling task and dataset were introduced by BIBREF4 . This was the first dataset specifically created for visual storytelling. They proposed a baseline approach which consists of a sequence to sequence model, where the encoder takes the sequence of images as input and the decoder takes the last state of the encoder as its first state to generate the story. Since this model produces stories with generic phrases, they used decode-time heuristics to improve the generated stories.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p0]] The decoder is the second LSTM network that uses the information obtained from the encoder to generate the sequence's story. The first input $x_0$ to the decoder is the image for which the text is being generated. The last hidden state from the encoder $h_e^{(t)}$ is used to initialize the first hidden state of the decoder $h_d^{(0)}$ . With this strategy, we provide the decoder with the context of the whole sequence and the content of the current image (i.e. global and local information) to generate the corresponding text that will contribute to the overall story.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p2]] Our proposed architecture is presented in Figure 3 . For each image in the sequence, we obtain its representation $\lbrace e(I_1),...,e(I_5)\rbrace $ using Inception v3. The encoder takes the images in order, one at every timestep $t$ . At time $t=5$ , we obtain the context vector through $h_e^{(t)}$ (represented by $\mathbf {Z}$ ). This vector is used to initialize each decoder's hidden state while the first input to each decoder is its corresponding image embedding $e(I_i)$ . Each decoder generates a sequence of words $\lbrace p_1,...,p_{n}\rbrace $ for each image in the sequence. The final story is the concatenation of the output of the 5 decoders.

The automatic evaluation was performed by computing the METEOR metric BIBREF5 on a public test set and a hidden test set. The latter consists of new stories generated by humans from a subset of image sequences of the public test set.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s0:p0]] Over the past few years, generating text from images and videos has gained a lot of attention in the Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing communities and several related tasks have been proposed, such as image labeling, image and video description and visual question answering. In particular, prominent results have been achieved in image description with various deep neural network architectures, e.g. BIBREF1 , BIBREF2 , BIBREF3 , BIBREF0 . However, the need of generating more narrative texts from images which may reflect experiences, rather than just listing objects and their attributes, has given rise to tasks such as visual storytelling BIBREF4 . This task is about generating a story from a sequence of images. Figure 1 shows the difference between descriptions of images in isolation and stories for images in sequence.

references.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s7:p0]] Our visual storyteller incorporates a context encoder and multiple independent decoders to the image description architecture by BIBREF0 to generate stories from image sequences. Having an independent decoder for each position of the image sequence, allowed our visual storyteller to build more specific language models using the context vector as its first state and the image embedding as its first input. In the internal track of the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018, we obtained competitive METEOR scores in both the public and hidden test sets and performed well in the human evaluation.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p1]] Our model contains five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence. All the 5 decoders use the last hidden state of the encoder (i.e. the context) as its first hidden state and take the corresponding image embedding as its first input. In this way, the first decoder generates the sequence of words for the first image in the sequence, the second decoder for the second image in the sequence, and so on. This allows each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence. For instance, the first decoder will learn the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder the closing sentences. The word embeddings were computed using word2vec BIBREF8 .

evaluationProducerReferences.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s7:p0]] Our visual storyteller incorporates a context encoder and multiple independent decoders to the image description architecture by BIBREF0 to generate stories from image sequences. Having an independent decoder for each position of the image sequence, allowed our visual storyteller to build more specific language models using the context vector as its first state and the image embedding as its first input. In the internal track of the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018, we obtained competitive METEOR scores in both the public and hidden test sets and performed well in the human evaluation.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p1]] Our model contains five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence. All the 5 decoders use the last hidden state of the encoder (i.e. the context) as its first hidden state and take the corresponding image embedding as its first input. In this way, the first decoder generates the sequence of words for the first image in the sequence, the second decoder for the second image in the sequence, and so on. This allows each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence. For instance, the first decoder will learn the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder the closing sentences. The word embeddings were computed using word2vec BIBREF8 .

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s3:p0]] The model's first component is a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), more precisely an LSTM that summarizes the sequence of images. At every timestep $t$ the network takes as input an image $I_i$ where $i\in \lbrace 1,2,3,4,5\rbrace $ from the sequence. At time $t=5$ , the LSTM has encoded the 5 images and provides the sequence's context through its last hidden state denoted by $h_e^{(t)}$ . The representation of the images was obtained through Inception V3.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s1:p1]] The visual storytelling task and dataset were introduced by BIBREF4 . This was the first dataset specifically created for visual storytelling. They proposed a baseline approach which consists of a sequence to sequence model, where the encoder takes the sequence of images as input and the decoder takes the last state of the encoder as its first state to generate the story. Since this model produces stories with generic phrases, they used decode-time heuristics to improve the generated stories.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p0]] The decoder is the second LSTM network that uses the information obtained from the encoder to generate the sequence's story. The first input $x_0$ to the decoder is the image for which the text is being generated. The last hidden state from the encoder $h_e^{(t)}$ is used to initialize the first hidden state of the decoder $h_d^{(0)}$ . With this strategy, we provide the decoder with the context of the whole sequence and the content of the current image (i.e. global and local information) to generate the corresponding text that will contribute to the overall story.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p2]] Our proposed architecture is presented in Figure 3 . For each image in the sequence, we obtain its representation $\lbrace e(I_1),...,e(I_5)\rbrace $ using Inception v3. The encoder takes the images in order, one at every timestep $t$ . At time $t=5$ , we obtain the context vector through $h_e^{(t)}$ (represented by $\mathbf {Z}$ ). This vector is used to initialize each decoder's hidden state while the first input to each decoder is its corresponding image embedding $e(I_i)$ . Each decoder generates a sequence of words $\lbrace p_1,...,p_{n}\rbrace $ for each image in the sequence. The final story is the concatenation of the output of the 5 decoders.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s5:p0]] The generated stories were evaluated using both automatic metrics and human ratings. The automatic evaluation was performed by computing the METEOR metric BIBREF5 on a public test set and a hidden test set. The former is a set of $1,938$ image sequences and stories taken from the test set of the VIST dataset BIBREF4 . The latter consists of new stories generated by humans from a subset of image sequences of the public test set.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s0:p0]] Over the past few years, generating text from images and videos has gained a lot of attention in the Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing communities and several related tasks have been proposed, such as image labeling, image and video description and visual question answering. In particular, prominent results have been achieved in image description with various deep neural network architectures, e.g. BIBREF1 , BIBREF2 , BIBREF3 , BIBREF0 . However, the need of generating more narrative texts from images which may reflect experiences, rather than just listing objects and their attributes, has given rise to tasks such as visual storytelling BIBREF4 . This task is about generating a story from a sequence of images. Figure 1 shows the difference between descriptions of images in isolation and stories for images in sequence.

questions.question: How is the sequential nature of the story captured?

result.answer:
The model captures the story's sequential nature through an encoder that processes the images in order, one at every timestep t; at t=5 it produces the context vector from the encoder's hidden state. [1][2]
Each image in the sequence is first represented using Inception v3, giving embeddings e(I_1) through e(I_5). [3][4]
The model has five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence. [5][6]
The encoder's context vector initializes each decoder's hidden state, and each decoder's first input is its corresponding image embedding. [7][6]
The first decoder generates the words for the first image, the second decoder for the second image, and so on, so each decoder learns a position-specific language model (e.g., the first learns opening sentences, the last closing sentences). [8][9][6]
Each decoder generates a word sequence for its image, and the final story is the concatenation of the outputs of the 5 decoders. [10][4]

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p2]] Our proposed architecture is presented in Figure 3 . For each image in the sequence, we obtain its representation $\lbrace e(I_1),...,e(I_5)\rbrace $ using Inception v3. The encoder takes the images in order, one at every timestep $t$ . At time $t=5$ , we obtain the context vector through $h_e^{(t)}$ (represented by $\mathbf {Z}$ ). This vector is used to initialize each decoder's hidden state while the first input to each decoder is its corresponding image embedding $e(I_i)$ . Each decoder generates a sequence of words $\lbrace p_1,...,p_{n}\rbrace $ for each image in the sequence. The final story is the concatenation of the output of the 5 decoders.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s1:p1]] The visual storytelling task and dataset were introduced by BIBREF4 . This was the first dataset specifically created for visual storytelling. They proposed a baseline approach which consists of a sequence to sequence model, where the encoder takes the sequence of images as input and the decoder takes the last state of the encoder as its first state to generate the story. Since this model produces stories with generic phrases, they used decode-time heuristics to improve the generated stories.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s0:p1]] In this paper, we describe the deep neural network architecture we used for the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018. The problem to solve in this challenge can be stated as follows: Given a sequence of 5 images, the system should output a story related to the content and events in the images. Our architecture is an extension of the image description architecture presented by BIBREF0 . We submitted the generated stories to the internal track of the Visual Storytelling (VIST) Challenge, which were evaluated using the METEOR metric BIBREF5 as well as human ratings.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s5:p1]] Human ratings of the stories were collected from crowd workers in Amazon Mechanical Turk. Only 200 stories were selected from the hidden test set for this evaluation. The crowd workers evaluated each story on a Likert scale with respect to 6 aspects: a) the story is focused, b) the story has good structure and coherence, c) would you share this story, d) do you think this story was written by a human, e) the story is visually grounded and f) the story is detailed. The crowd workers were also asked to evaluate stories generated by humans for comparison purposes.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p0]] The decoder is the second LSTM network that uses the information obtained from the encoder to generate the sequence's story. The first input $x_0$ to the decoder is the image for which the text is being generated. The last hidden state from the encoder $h_e^{(t)}$ is used to initialize the first hidden state of the decoder $h_d^{(0)}$ . With this strategy, we provide the decoder with the context of the whole sequence and the content of the current image (i.e. global and local information) to generate the corresponding text that will contribute to the overall story.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s5:p0]] The generated stories were evaluated using both automatic metrics and human ratings. The automatic evaluation was performed by computing the METEOR metric BIBREF5 on a public test set and a hidden test set. The former is a set of $1,938$ image sequences and stories taken from the test set of the VIST dataset BIBREF4 . The latter consists of new stories generated by humans from a subset of image sequences of the public test set.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p1]] Our model contains five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence. All the 5 decoders use the last hidden state of the encoder (i.e. the context) as its first hidden state and take the corresponding image embedding as its first input. In this way, the first decoder generates the sequence of words for the first image in the sequence, the second decoder for the second image in the sequence, and so on. This allows each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence. For instance, the first decoder will learn the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder the closing sentences. The word embeddings were computed using word2vec BIBREF8 .

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s3:p0]] The model's first component is a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), more precisely an LSTM that summarizes the sequence of images. At every timestep $t$ the network takes as input an image $I_i$ where $i\in \lbrace 1,2,3,4,5\rbrace $ from the sequence. At time $t=5$ , the LSTM has encoded the 5 images and provides the sequence's context through its last hidden state denoted by $h_e^{(t)}$ . The representation of the images was obtained through Inception V3.

content.text: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p2]] Our proposed architecture is presented in Figure 3 . For each image in the sequence, we obtain its representation $\lbrace e(I_1),...,e(I_5)\rbrace $ using Inception v3. The encoder takes the images in order, one at every timestep $t$ . At time $t=5$ , we obtain the context vector through $h_e^{(t)}$ (represented by $\mathbf {Z}$ ). This vector is used to initialize each decoder's hidden state while the first input to each decoder is its corresponding image embedding $e(I_i)$ . Each decoder generates a sequence of words $\lbrace p_1,...
,p_{n}\rbrace $ for each image in the sequence. The final story is the concatenation of the output of the 5 decoders.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s1:p1]] The visual storytelling task and dataset were introduced by BIBREF4 . This was the first dataset specifically created for visual storytelling. They proposed a baseline approach which consists of a sequence to sequence model, where the encoder takes the sequence of images as input and the decoder takes the last state of the encoder as its first state to generate the story. Since this model produces stories with generic phrases, they used decode-time heuristics to improve the generated stories.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s0:p1]] In this paper, we describe the deep neural network architecture we used for the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018. The problem to solve in this challenge can be stated as follows: Given a sequence of 5 images, the system should output a story related to the content and events in the images. Our architecture is an extension of the image description architecture presented by BIBREF0 . We submitted the generated stories to the internal track of the Visual Storytelling (VIST) Challenge, which were evaluated using the METEOR metric BIBREF5 as well as human ratings.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s5:p1]] Human ratings of the stories were collected from crowd workers in Amazon Mechanical Turk. Only 200 stories were selected from the hidden test set for this evaluation. The crowd workers evaluated each story on a Likert scale with respect to 6 aspects: a) the story is focused, b) the story has good structure and coherence, c) would you share this story, d) do you think this story was written by a human, e) the story is visually grounded and f) the story is detailed. The crowd workers were also asked to evaluate stories generated by humans for comparison purposes.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p0]] The decoder is the second LSTM network that uses the information obtained from the encoder to generate the sequence's story. The first input $x_0$ to the decoder is the image for which the text is being generated. The last hidden state from the encoder $h_e^{(t)}$ is used to initialize the first hidden state of the decoder $h_d^{(0)}$ . With this strategy, we provide the decoder with the context of the whole sequence and the content of the current image (i.e. global and local information) to generate the corresponding text that will contribute to the overall story.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s5:p0]] The generated stories were evaluated using both automatic metrics and human ratings. The automatic evaluation was performed by computing the METEOR metric BIBREF5 on a public test set and a hidden test set. The former is a set of $1,938$ image sequences and stories taken from the test set of the VIST dataset BIBREF4 . The latter consists of new stories generated by humans from a subset of image sequences of the public test set.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p1]] Our model contains five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence. All the 5 decoders use the last hidden state of the encoder (i.e. the context) as its first hidden state and take the corresponding image embedding as its first input. In this way, the first decoder generates the sequence of words for the first image in the sequence, the second decoder for the second image in the sequence, and so on. This allows each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence.
For instance, the first decoder will learn the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder the closing sentences. The word embeddings were computed using word2vec BIBREF8 .

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s3:p0]] The model's first component is a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), more precisely an LSTM that summarizes the sequence of images. At every timestep $t$ the network takes as input an image $I_i$ where $i\in \lbrace 1,2,3,4,5\rbrace $ from the sequence. At time $t=5$ , the LSTM has encoded the 5 images and provides the sequence's context through its last hidden state denoted by $h_e^{(t)}$ . The representation of the images was obtained through Inception V3.

claims.text: The model captures the story's sequential nature through an encoder that processes the images in order, one at every timestep t; at t=5 it produces the context vector from the encoder's hidden state.
Each image in the sequence is first represented using Inception v3, giving embeddings e(I_1) through e(I_5).
The model has five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence.
The encoder's context vector initializes each decoder's hidden state, and each decoder's first input is its corresponding image embedding.

The first decoder generates the words for the first image, the second decoder for the second image, and so on, so each decoder learns a position-specific language model (e.g., the first learns opening sentences, the last closing sentences).
Each decoder generates a word sequence for its image, and the final story is the concatenation of the outputs of the 5 decoders.

result.answer:
模型首先用 Inception v3 为序列中每张图像取得表示 {e(I1),…,e(I5)}。 [1][2]
编码器按顺序在每个时间步 t 输入一张图像，在 t=5 时通过最后隐藏状态 h_e^(t)（记为 Z）得到整个序列的上下文向量。 [3][4]
该上下文向量用于初始化每个解码器的隐藏状态，而每个解码器的第一个输入是其对应图像的嵌入 e(I_i)。 [5][6]
模型包含五个独立解码器，每个图像位置一个；第一个解码器为第一张图像生成词序列，第二个为第二张，依此类推。 [7][8]
每个解码器为序列中对应图像生成一段词序列 {p1,…,pn}，最终故事是 5 个解码器输出的拼接。 [9][2]
这种按位置独立的解码器使每个解码器能为序列的每个位置学习特定的语言模型，例如第一个解码器学习故事开头句、最后一个学习结尾句。 [10][6]

For each image in the sequence, we obtain its representation $\lbrace e(I_1),...,e(I_5)\rbrace $ using Inception v3. The encoder takes the images in order, one at every timestep $t$ . At time $t=5$ , we obtain the context vector through $h_e^{(t)}$ (represented by $\mathbf {Z}$ ). This vector is used to initialize each decoder's hidden state while the first input to each decoder is its corresponding image embedding $e(I_i)$ . Each decoder generates a sequence of words $\lbrace p_1,...,p_{n}\rbrace $ for each image in the sequence. The final story is the concatenation of the output of the 5 decoders.

evidence.sourceTitle: Contextualize, Show and Tell: A Neural Visual Storyteller
evidence.text: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p1]] Our model contains five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence. All the 5 decoders use the last hidden state of the encoder (i.e. the context) as its first hidden state and take the corresponding image embedding as its first input. In this way, the first decoder generates the sequence of words for the first image in the sequence, the second decoder for the second image in the sequence, and so on. This allows each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence. For instance, the first decoder will learn the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder the closing sentences. The word embeddings were computed using word2vec BIBREF8 .

evidence.text: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s0:p1]] In this paper, we describe the deep neural network architecture we used for the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018. The problem to solve in this challenge can be stated as follows: Given a sequence of 5 images, the system should output a story related to the content and events in the images. Our architecture is an extension of the image description architecture presented by BIBREF0 . We submitted the generated stories to the internal track of the Visual Storytelling (VIST) Challenge, which were evaluated using the METEOR metric BIBREF5 as well as human ratings.

conditions: Given a sequence of 5 images

evidence.text: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p0]] The decoder is the second LSTM network that uses the information obtained from the encoder to generate the sequence's story. The first input $x_0$ to the decoder is the image for which the text is being generated. The last hidden state from the encoder $h_e^{(t)}$ is used to initialize the first hidden state of the decoder $h_d^{(0)}$ . With this strategy, we provide the decoder with the context of the whole sequence and the content of the current image (i.e. global and local information) to generate the corresponding text that will contribute to the overall story.

evidence.text: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s7:p0]] Our visual storyteller incorporates a context encoder and multiple independent decoders to the image description architecture by BIBREF0 to generate stories from image sequences. All the 5 decoders use the last hidden state of the encoder (i.e. the context) as its first hidden state and take the corresponding image embedding as its first input. In this way, the first decoder generates the sequence of words for the first image in the sequence, the second decoder for the second image in the sequence, and so on. This allows each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence. For instance, the first decoder will learn the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder the closing sentences. The word embeddings were computed using word2vec BIBREF8 .

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p2]] Our proposed architecture is presented in Figure 3 . For each image in the sequence, we obtain its representation $\lbrace e(I_1),...,e(I_5)\rbrace $ using Inception v3. The encoder takes the images in order, one at every timestep $t$ . At time $t=5$ , we obtain the context vector through $h_e^{(t)}$ (represented by $\mathbf {Z}$ ). This vector is used to initialize each decoder's hidden state while the first input to each decoder is its corresponding image embedding $e(I_i)$ . Each decoder generates a sequence of words $\lbrace p_1,...,p_{n}\rbrace $ for each image in the sequence. The final story is the concatenation of the output of the 5 decoders.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s0:p1]] In this paper, we describe the deep neural network architecture we used for the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018. The problem to solve in this challenge can be stated as follows: Given a sequence of 5 images, the system should output a story related to the content and events in the images. Our architecture is an extension of the image description architecture presented by BIBREF0 . We submitted the generated stories to the internal track of the Visual Storytelling (VIST) Challenge, which were evaluated using the METEOR metric BIBREF5 as well as human ratings.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s5:p1]] Human ratings of the stories were collected from crowd workers in Amazon Mechanical Turk. Only 200 stories were selected from the hidden test set for this evaluation. The crowd workers evaluated each story on a Likert scale with respect to 6 aspects: a) the story is focused, b) the story has good structure and coherence, c) would you share this story, d) do you think this story was written by a human, e) the story is visually grounded and f) the story is detailed. The crowd workers were also asked to evaluate stories generated by humans for comparison purposes.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p1]] Our model contains five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence. All the 5 decoders use the last hidden state of the encoder (i.e. the context) as its first hidden state and take the corresponding image embedding as its first input. In this way, the first decoder generates the sequence of words for the first image in the sequence, the second decoder for the second image in the sequence, and so on. This allows each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence. For instance, the first decoder will learn the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder the closing sentences. The word embeddings were computed using word2vec BIBREF8 .

answerClaimProvenance.text: 模型首先用 Inception v3 为序列中每张图像取得表示 {e(I1),…,e(I5)}。
编码器按顺序在每个时间步 t 输入一张图像，在 t=5 时通过最后隐藏状态 h_e^(t)（记为 Z）得到整个序列的上下文向量。

模型包含五个独立解码器，每个图像位置一个；第一个解码器为第一张图像生成词序列，第二个为第二张，依此类推。
每个解码器为序列中对应图像生成一段词序列 {p1,…,pn}，最终故事是 5 个解码器输出的拼接。
这种按位置独立的解码器使每个解码器能为序列的每个位置学习特定的语言模型，例如第一个解码器学习故事开头句、最后一个学习结尾句。

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s2:p0]] Our model extends the image description model by BIBREF0 , which consists of an encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder is a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and the decoder is a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, as presented in Figure 2 . The image is passed through the encoder generating the image representation that is used by the decoder to know the content of the image and generate the description word by word. In the following, we describe how we extended this model for the visual storytelling task.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s1:p1]] The visual storytelling task and dataset were introduced by BIBREF4 . This was the first dataset specifically created for visual storytelling. They proposed a baseline approach which consists of a sequence to sequence model, where the encoder takes the sequence of images as input and the decoder takes the last state of the encoder as its first state to generate the story. Since this model produces stories with generic phrases, they used decode-time heuristics to improve the generated stories.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p0]] The decoder is the second LSTM network that uses the information obtained from the encoder to generate the sequence's story. The first input $x_0$ to the decoder is the image for which the text is being generated. The last hidden state from the encoder $h_e^{(t)}$ is used to initialize the first hidden state of the decoder $h_d^{(0)}$ . With this strategy, we provide the decoder with the context of the whole sequence and the content of the current image (i.e. global and local information) to generate the corresponding text that will contribute to the overall story.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p2]] Our proposed architecture is presented in Figure 3 . For each image in the sequence, we obtain its representation $\lbrace e(I_1),...,e(I_5)\rbrace $ using Inception v3. The encoder takes the images in order, one at every timestep $t$ . At time $t=5$ , we obtain the context vector through $h_e^{(t)}$ (represented by $\mathbf {Z}$ ). This vector is used to initialize each decoder's hidden state while the first input to each decoder is its corresponding image embedding $e(I_i)$ . Each decoder generates a sequence of words $\lbrace p_1,...,p_{n}\rbrace $ for each image in the sequence. The final story is the concatenation of the output of the 5 decoders.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p1]] Our model contains five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence. All the 5 decoders use the last hidden state of the encoder (i.e. the context) as its first hidden state and take the corresponding image embedding as its first input. In this way, the first decoder generates the sequence of words for the first image in the sequence, the second decoder for the second image in the sequence, and so on. This allows each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence. For instance, the first decoder will learn the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder the closing sentences. The word embeddings were computed using word2vec BIBREF8 .

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s3:p0]] The model's first component is a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), more precisely an LSTM that summarizes the sequence of images. At every timestep $t$ the network takes as input an image $I_i$ where $i\in \lbrace 1,2,3,4,5\rbrace $ from the sequence. At time $t=5$ , the LSTM has encoded the 5 images and provides the sequence's context through its last hidden state denoted by $h_e^{(t)}$ . The representation of the images was obtained through Inception V3.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s7:p0]] Our visual storyteller incorporates a context encoder and multiple independent decoders to the image description architecture by BIBREF0 to generate stories from image sequences. Having an independent decoder for each position of the image sequence, allowed our visual storyteller to build more specific language models using the context vector as its first state and the image embedding as its first input. In the internal track of the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018, we obtained competitive METEOR scores in both the public and hidden test sets and performed well in the human evaluation.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s0:p1]] In this paper, we describe the deep neural network architecture we used for the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018. The problem to solve in this challenge can be stated as follows: Given a sequence of 5 images, the system should output a story related to the content and events in the images. Our architecture is an extension of the image description architecture presented by BIBREF0 . We submitted the generated stories to the internal track of the Visual Storytelling (VIST) Challenge, which were evaluated using the METEOR metric BIBREF5 as well as human ratings.

evidence.text: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s0:p1]] In this paper, we describe the deep neural network architecture we used for the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018. The problem to solve in this challenge can be stated as follows: Given a sequence of 5 images, the system should output a story related to the content and events in the images. Our architecture is an extension of the image description architecture presented by BIBREF0 . We submitted the generated stories to the internal track of the Visual Storytelling (VIST) Challenge, which were evaluated using the METEOR metric BIBREF5 as well as human ratings.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s2:p0]] Our model extends the image description model by BIBREF0 , which consists of an encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder is a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and the decoder is a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, as presented in Figure 2 . The image is passed through the encoder generating the image representation that is used by the decoder to know the content of the image and generate the description word by word. In the following, we describe how we extended this model for the visual storytelling task.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s1:p1]] The visual storytelling task and dataset were introduced by BIBREF4 . This was the first dataset specifically created for visual storytelling. They proposed a baseline approach which consists of a sequence to sequence model, where the encoder takes the sequence of images as input and the decoder takes the last state of the encoder as its first state to generate the story. Since this model produces stories with generic phrases, they used decode-time heuristics to improve the generated stories.

references.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s2:p0]] Our model extends the image description model by BIBREF0 , which consists of an encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder is a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and the decoder is a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, as presented in Figure 2 . The image is passed through the encoder generating the image representation that is used by the decoder to know the content of the image and generate the description word by word. In the following, we describe how we extended this model for the visual storytelling task.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s1:p1]] The visual storytelling task and dataset were introduced by BIBREF4 . This was the first dataset specifically created for visual storytelling. They proposed a baseline approach which consists of a sequence to sequence model, where the encoder takes the sequence of images as input and the decoder takes the last state of the encoder as its first state to generate the story. Since this model produces stories with generic phrases, they used decode-time heuristics to improve the generated stories.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p0]] The decoder is the second LSTM network that uses the information obtained from the encoder to generate the sequence's story. The first input $x_0$ to the decoder is the image for which the text is being generated. The last hidden state from the encoder $h_e^{(t)}$ is used to initialize the first hidden state of the decoder $h_d^{(0)}$ . With this strategy, we provide the decoder with the context of the whole sequence and the content of the current image (i.e. global and local information) to generate the corresponding text that will contribute to the overall story.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p2]] Our proposed architecture is presented in Figure 3 . For each image in the sequence, we obtain its representation $\lbrace e(I_1),...,e(I_5)\rbrace $ using Inception v3. The encoder takes the images in order, one at every timestep $t$ . At time $t=5$ , we obtain the context vector through $h_e^{(t)}$ (represented by $\mathbf {Z}$ ). This vector is used to initialize each decoder's hidden state while the first input to each decoder is its corresponding image embedding $e(I_i)$ . Each decoder generates a sequence of words $\lbrace p_1,...,p_{n}\rbrace $ for each image in the sequence. The final story is the concatenation of the output of the 5 decoders.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p1]] Our model contains five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence. All the 5 decoders use the last hidden state of the encoder (i.e. the context) as its first hidden state and take the corresponding image embedding as its first input. In this way, the first decoder generates the sequence of words for the first image in the sequence, the second decoder for the second image in the sequence, and so on. This allows each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence. For instance, the first decoder will learn the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder the closing sentences. The word embeddings were computed using word2vec BIBREF8 .

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s3:p0]] The model's first component is a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), more precisely an LSTM that summarizes the sequence of images. At every timestep $t$ the network takes as input an image $I_i$ where $i\in \lbrace 1,2,3,4,5\rbrace $ from the sequence. At time $t=5$ , the LSTM has encoded the 5 images and provides the sequence's context through its last hidden state denoted by $h_e^{(t)}$ . The representation of the images was obtained through Inception V3.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s7:p0]] Our visual storyteller incorporates a context encoder and multiple independent decoders to the image description architecture by BIBREF0 to generate stories from image sequences. Having an independent decoder for each position of the image sequence, allowed our visual storyteller to build more specific language models using the context vector as its first state and the image embedding as its first input. In the internal track of the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018, we obtained competitive METEOR scores in both the public and hidden test sets and performed well in the human evaluation.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s0:p1]] In this paper, we describe the deep neural network architecture we used for the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018. The problem to solve in this challenge can be stated as follows: Given a sequence of 5 images, the system should output a story related to the content and events in the images. Our architecture is an extension of the image description architecture presented by BIBREF0 . We submitted the generated stories to the internal track of the Visual Storytelling (VIST) Challenge, which were evaluated using the METEOR metric BIBREF5 as well as human ratings.

In the following, we describe how we extended this model for the visual storytelling task.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p0]] The decoder is the second LSTM network that uses the information obtained from the encoder to generate the sequence's story. The first input $x_0$ to the decoder is the image for which the text is being generated. The last hidden state from the encoder $h_e^{(t)}$ is used to initialize the first hidden state of the decoder $h_d^{(0)}$ . With this strategy, we provide the decoder with the context of the whole sequence and the content of the current image (i.e. global and local information) to generate the corresponding text that will contribute to the overall story.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p1]] Our model contains five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence. All the 5 decoders use the last hidden state of the encoder (i.e. the context) as its first hidden state and take the corresponding image embedding as its first input. In this way, the first decoder generates the sequence of words for the first image in the sequence, the second decoder for the second image in the sequence, and so on. This allows each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence. For instance, the first decoder will learn the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder the closing sentences. The word embeddings were computed using word2vec BIBREF8 .

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s7:p0]] Our visual storyteller incorporates a context encoder and multiple independent decoders to the image description architecture by BIBREF0 to generate stories from image sequences. Having an independent decoder for each position of the image sequence, allowed our visual storyteller to build more specific language models using the context vector as its first state and the image embedding as its first input. In the internal track of the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018, we obtained competitive METEOR scores in both the public and hidden test sets and performed well in the human evaluation.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s3:p0]] The model's first component is a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), more precisely an LSTM that summarizes the sequence of images. At every timestep $t$ the network takes as input an image $I_i$ where $i\in \lbrace 1,2,3,4,5\rbrace $ from the sequence. At time $t=5$ , the LSTM has encoded the 5 images and provides the sequence's context through its last hidden state denoted by $h_e^{(t)}$ . The representation of the images was obtained through Inception V3.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s2:p0]] Our model extends the image description model by BIBREF0 , which consists of an encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder is a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and the decoder is a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, as presented in Figure 2 . The image is passed through the encoder generating the image representation that is used by the decoder to know the content of the image and generate the description word by word. In the following, we describe how we extended this model for the visual storytelling task.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p2]] Our proposed architecture is presented in Figure 3 . For each image in the sequence, we obtain its representation $\lbrace e(I_1),...,e(I_5)\rbrace $ using Inception v3. The encoder takes the images in order, one at every timestep $t$ . At time $t=5$ , we obtain the context vector through $h_e^{(t)}$ (represented by $\mathbf {Z}$ ). This vector is used to initialize each decoder's hidden state while the first input to each decoder is its corresponding image embedding $e(I_i)$ . Each decoder generates a sequence of words $\lbrace p_1,...,p_{n}\rbrace $ for each image in the sequence. The final story is the concatenation of the output of the 5 decoders.

evaluationProducerReferences.content: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s7:p1]] In the future, we plan to explore the use of an attention mechanism or a bidirectional LSTM to cope with repetitive phrases within the same story.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p0]] The decoder is the second LSTM network that uses the information obtained from the encoder to generate the sequence's story. The first input $x_0$ to the decoder is the image for which the text is being generated. The last hidden state from the encoder $h_e^{(t)}$ is used to initialize the first hidden state of the decoder $h_d^{(0)}$ . With this strategy, we provide the decoder with the context of the whole sequence and the content of the current image (i.e. global and local information) to generate the corresponding text that will contribute to the overall story.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p1]] Our model contains five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence. All the 5 decoders use the last hidden state of the encoder (i.e. the context) as its first hidden state and take the corresponding image embedding as its first input. In this way, the first decoder generates the sequence of words for the first image in the sequence, the second decoder for the second image in the sequence, and so on. This allows each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence. For instance, the first decoder will learn the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder the closing sentences. The word embeddings were computed using word2vec BIBREF8 .

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s1:p1]] The visual storytelling task and dataset were introduced by BIBREF4 . This was the first dataset specifically created for visual storytelling. They proposed a baseline approach which consists of a sequence to sequence model, where the encoder takes the sequence of images as input and the decoder takes the last state of the encoder as its first state to generate the story. Since this model produces stories with generic phrases, they used decode-time heuristics to improve the generated stories.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s7:p0]] Our visual storyteller incorporates a context encoder and multiple independent decoders to the image description architecture by BIBREF0 to generate stories from image sequences. Having an independent decoder for each position of the image sequence, allowed our visual storyteller to build more specific language models using the context vector as its first state and the image embedding as its first input. In the internal track of the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018, we obtained competitive METEOR scores in both the public and hidden test sets and performed well in the human evaluation.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s3:p0]] The model's first component is a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), more precisely an LSTM that summarizes the sequence of images. At every timestep $t$ the network takes as input an image $I_i$ where $i\in \lbrace 1,2,3,4,5\rbrace $ from the sequence. At time $t=5$ , the LSTM has encoded the 5 images and provides the sequence's context through its last hidden state denoted by $h_e^{(t)}$ . The representation of the images was obtained through Inception V3.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s2:p0]] Our model extends the image description model by BIBREF0 , which consists of an encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder is a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and the decoder is a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, as presented in Figure 2 . The image is passed through the encoder generating the image representation that is used by the decoder to know the content of the image and generate the description word by word. In the following, we describe how we extended this model for the visual storytelling task.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p2]] Our proposed architecture is presented in Figure 3 . For each image in the sequence, we obtain its representation $\lbrace e(I_1),...,e(I_5)\rbrace $ using Inception v3. The encoder takes the images in order, one at every timestep $t$ . At time $t=5$ , we obtain the context vector through $h_e^{(t)}$ (represented by $\mathbf {Z}$ ). This vector is used to initialize each decoder's hidden state while the first input to each decoder is its corresponding image embedding $e(I_i)$ . Each decoder generates a sequence of words $\lbrace p_1,...,p_{n}\rbrace $ for each image in the sequence. The final story is the concatenation of the output of the 5 decoders.

evidence.text: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s0:p1]] In this paper, we describe the deep neural network architecture we used for the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018. The problem to solve in this challenge can be stated as follows: Given a sequence of 5 images, the system should output a story related to the content and events in the images. Our architecture is an extension of the image description architecture presented by BIBREF0 . We submitted the generated stories to the internal track of the Visual Storytelling (VIST) Challenge, which were evaluated using the METEOR metric BIBREF5 as well as human ratings.

In this way, the first decoder generates the sequence of words for the first image in the sequence, the second decoder for the second image in the sequence, and so on. This allows each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence. For instance, the first decoder will learn the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder the closing sentences. The word embeddings were computed using word2vec BIBREF8 .

evidence.text: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p2]] Our proposed architecture is presented in Figure 3 . For each image in the sequence, we obtain its representation $\lbrace e(I_1),...,e(I_5)\rbrace $ using Inception v3. The encoder takes the images in order, one at every timestep $t$ . At time $t=5$ , we obtain the context vector through $h_e^{(t)}$ (represented by $\mathbf {Z}$ ). This vector is used to initialize each decoder's hidden state while the first input to each decoder is its corresponding image embedding $e(I_i)$ . Each decoder generates a sequence of words $\lbrace p_1,...,p_{n}\rbrace $ for each image in the sequence. The final story is the concatenation of the output of the 5 decoders.

evidence.text: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s5:p1]] Human ratings of the stories were collected from crowd workers in Amazon Mechanical Turk. The crowd workers evaluated each story on a Likert scale with respect to 6 aspects: a) the story is focused, b) the story has good structure and coherence, c) would you share this story, d) do you think this story was written by a human, e) the story is visually grounded and f) the story is detailed. The crowd workers were also asked to evaluate stories generated by humans for comparison purposes.

evidence.text: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s6:p3]] Figure 4 shows some sample stories generated by our model from the public test set of the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018. Although some of the generated stories are grammatically correct and coherent, they tend to contain repetitive phrases or ideas. We can also observe that some stories are not nearly related to the actual content of the images or include generic phrases like This is a picture of a store. These limitations of our model reflected on the ratings of the visually grounded and detailed aspects of the human evaluation.

segments.text: [[QASPER:1806.00738:s0:p0]] Over the past few years, generating text from images and videos has gained a lot of attention in the Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing communities and several related tasks have been proposed, such as image labeling, image and video description and visual question answering. In particular, prominent results have been achieved in image description with various deep neural network architectures, e.g. BIBREF1 , BIBREF2 , BIBREF3 , BIBREF0 . However, the need of generating more narrative texts from images which may reflect experiences, rather than just listing objects and their attributes, has given rise to tasks such as visual storytelling BIBREF4 . This task is about generating a story from a sequence of images. Figure 1 shows the difference between descriptions of images in isolation and stories for images in sequence.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s0:p1]] In this paper, we describe the deep neural network architecture we used for the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018. The problem to solve in this challenge can be stated as follows: Given a sequence of 5 images, the system should output a story related to the content and events in the images. Our architecture is an extension of the image description architecture presented by BIBREF0 . We submitted the generated stories to the internal track of the Visual Storytelling (VIST) Challenge, which were evaluated using the METEOR metric BIBREF5 as well as human ratings.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s1:p0]] The work by BIBREF6 presented probably the first system for generating stories from an album of images. This early approach involved the use of the NYC and Disney datasets mined from blog posts by the authors.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s1:p1]] The visual storytelling task and dataset were introduced by BIBREF4 . This was the first dataset specifically created for visual storytelling. They proposed a baseline approach which consists of a sequence to sequence model, where the encoder takes the sequence of images as input and the decoder takes the last state of the encoder as its first state to generate the story. Since this model produces stories with generic phrases, they used decode-time heuristics to improve the generated stories.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s1:p2]]  BIBREF7 presented a multi-task model that performs album summarization and story generation. Even though the model achieved state-of-the-art scores on the VIST dataset with different metrics, some of the sample stories presented in the paper are incoherent.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s2:p0]] Our model extends the image description model by BIBREF0 , which consists of an encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder is a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and the decoder is a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, as presented in Figure 2 . The image is passed through the encoder generating the image representation that is used by the decoder to know the content of the image and generate the description word by word. In the following, we describe how we extended this model for the visual storytelling task.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s3:p0]] The model's first component is a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), more precisely an LSTM that summarizes the sequence of images. At every timestep $t$ the network takes as input an image $I_i$ where $i\in \lbrace 1,2,3,4,5\rbrace $ from the sequence. At time $t=5$ , the LSTM has encoded the 5 images and provides the sequence's context through its last hidden state denoted by $h_e^{(t)}$ . The representation of the images was obtained through Inception V3.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p0]] The decoder is the second LSTM network that uses the information obtained from the encoder to generate the sequence's story. The first input $x_0$ to the decoder is the image for which the text is being generated. The last hidden state from the encoder $h_e^{(t)}$ is used to initialize the first hidden state of the decoder $h_d^{(0)}$ . With this strategy, we provide the decoder with the context of the whole sequence and the content of the current image (i.e. global and local information) to generate the corresponding text that will contribute to the overall story.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p1]] Our model contains five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence. All the 5 decoders use the last hidden state of the encoder (i.e. the context) as its first hidden state and take the corresponding image embedding as its first input. In this way, the first decoder generates the sequence of words for the first image in the sequence, the second decoder for the second image in the sequence, and so on. This allows each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence. For instance, the first decoder will learn the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder the closing sentences. The word embeddings were computed using word2vec BIBREF8 .

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s4:p2]] Our proposed architecture is presented in Figure 3 . For each image in the sequence, we obtain its representation $\lbrace e(I_1),...,e(I_5)\rbrace $ using Inception v3. The encoder takes the images in order, one at every timestep $t$ . At time $t=5$ , we obtain the context vector through $h_e^{(t)}$ (represented by $\mathbf {Z}$ ). This vector is used to initialize each decoder's hidden state while the first input to each decoder is its corresponding image embedding $e(I_i)$ . Each decoder generates a sequence of words $\lbrace p_1,...,p_{n}\rbrace $ for each image in the sequence. The final story is the concatenation of the output of the 5 decoders.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s5:p0]] The generated stories were evaluated using both automatic metrics and human ratings. The automatic evaluation was performed by computing the METEOR metric BIBREF5 on a public test set and a hidden test set. The former is a set of $1,938$ image sequences and stories taken from the test set of the VIST dataset BIBREF4 . The latter consists of new stories generated by humans from a subset of image sequences of the public test set.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s5:p1]] Human ratings of the stories were collected from crowd workers in Amazon Mechanical Turk. Only 200 stories were selected from the hidden test set for this evaluation. The crowd workers evaluated each story on a Likert scale with respect to 6 aspects: a) the story is focused, b) the story has good structure and coherence, c) would you share this story, d) do you think this story was written by a human, e) the story is visually grounded and f) the story is detailed. The crowd workers were also asked to evaluate stories generated by humans for comparison purposes.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s6:p0]] Table 1 shows the METEOR scores by our model in the public and hidden test set of the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018. Table 2 presents results of the human evaluation. Our model achieved competitive METEOR scores in both test sets and performed well in the human evaluation.
[[QASPER:1806.00738:s6:p1]] An evaluation over the complete VIST test set was also performed and the results are shown in Table 3 .
[[QASPER:1806.00738:s6:p2]] Our model obtained the highest scores with the METEOR and BLEU-3 metrics but lagged behind the model by BIBREF7 with the ROUGE and CIDEr metrics.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s6:p3]] Figure 4 shows some sample stories generated by our model from the public test set of the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018. Although some of the generated stories are grammatically correct and coherent, they tend to contain repetitive phrases or ideas. We can also observe that some stories are not nearly related to the actual content of the images or include generic phrases like This is a picture of a store. These limitations of our model reflected on the ratings of the visually grounded and detailed aspects of the human evaluation.

[[QASPER:1806.00738:s7:p0]] Our visual storyteller incorporates a context encoder and multiple independent decoders to the image description architecture by BIBREF0 to generate stories from image sequences. Having an independent decoder for each position of the image sequence, allowed our visual storyteller to build more specific language models using the context vector as its first state and the image embedding as its first input. In the internal track of the Visual Storytelling Challenge 2018, we obtained competitive METEOR scores in both the public and hidden test sets and performed well in the human evaluation.
[[QASPER:1806.00738:s7:p1]] In the future, we plan to explore the use of an attention mechanism or a bidirectional LSTM to cope with repetitive phrases within the same story.
[[QASPER:1806.00738:s8:p0]] This research is supported by the PAPIIT-UNAM research grant IA104016. Diana González Rico is supported by CONACYT.

result.answer:

citations.content: [[QASPER:1603.01514:s8:p0]] Following titovcrosslingual, we run our experiments on the English (EN) and German (DE) sections of the CoNLL 2009 corpus BIBREF13 , and EN-DE section of the Europarl corpus BIBREF14 . We get about 40k EN and 36k DE sentences from the CoNLL 2009 training set, and about 1.5M parallel EN-DE sentences from Europarl. For appropriate comparison, we keep the same setting as in BIBREF6 for automatic parses and argument identification, which we briefly describe here. The EN sentences are parsed syntactically using MaltParser BIBREF15 and DE using LTH parser BIBREF16 . All the non-auxiliary verbs are selected as predicates. In CoNLL data, this gives us about 3k EN and 500 DE predicates. The total number of predicate instances are 3.4M in EN (89k CoNLL + 3.3M Europarl) and 2.62M in DE (17k CoNLL + 2.6M Europarl). The arguments for EN are identified using the heuristics proposed by lang2011unsupervised. However, we get an F1 score of 85.1% for argument identification on CoNLL 2009 EN data as opposed to 80.7% reported by titovcrosslingual. This could be due to implementation differences, which unfortunately makes our EN results incomparable. For DE, the arguments are identified using the LTH system BIBREF16 , which gives an F1 score of 86.5% on the CoNLL 2009 DE data. The word alignments for the EN-DE parallel Europarl corpus are computed using GIZA++ BIBREF17 . For high-precision, only the intersecting alignments in the two directions are kept. We define two semantic arguments as aligned if their head-words are aligned. In total we get 9.3M arguments for EN (240k CoNLL + 9.1M Europarl) and 4.43M for DE (32k CoNLL + 4.4M Europarl). Out of these, 0.76M arguments are aligned.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1603.01514:s13:p0]] We propose a Bayesian model of semantic role induction (SRI) that uses crosslingual latent variables to capture role alignments in parallel corpora. The crosslingual latent variables capture correlations between roles in different languages, and regularize the parameter estimates of the monolingual models. Because this is a joint Bayesian model of multilingual SRI, we can apply the same model to a variety of training scenarios just by changing the inference procedure appropriately. We evaluate monolingual SRI with a large unlabeled dataset, bilingual SRI with a parallel corpus, bilingual SRI with annotations available for the source language, and monolingual SRI with a small labeled dataset. Increasing the amount of monolingual unlabeled data significantly improves SRI in German but not in English. Adding word alignments in parallel sentences results in small, non significant improvements, even if there is some labeled data available in the source language. This difficulty in showing the usefulness of parallel corpora for SRI may be due to the current assumptions about role alignments, which mean that only a small percentage of roles are aligned. Further analyses reveals that annotating small amounts of data can easily outperform the performance gains obtained by adding large unlabeled dataset as well as adding parallel corpora.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1603.01514:s3:p0]] The multilingual model uses word alignments between sentences in a parallel corpus to exploit role correspondences across languages. We make copies of the monolingual model for each language and add additional crosslingual latent variables (CLVs) to couple the monolingual models, capturing crosslingual semantic role patterns. Concretely, when training on parallel sentences, whenever the head words of the arguments are aligned, we add a CLV as a parent of the two corresponding role variables. Figure FIGREF16 illustrates this model. The generative process, as explained below, remains the same as the monolingual model for the most part, with the exception of aligned roles which are now generated by both the monolingual process as well as the CLV.

sourcePassages.content: [[QASPER:1603.01514:s12:p1]] For monolingual unsupervised SRL, swier2004unsupervised presented the first work on a domain-general corpus, the British National Corpus, using 54 verbs taken from VerbNet. garg2012unsupervised proposed a Bayesian model for this problem that we use here. titov2012bayesian also proposed a closely related Bayesian model. grenager2006unsupervised proposed a generative model but their parameter space consisted of all possible linkings of syntactic constituents and semantic roles, which made unsupervised learning difficult and a separate language-specific rule based method had to be used to constrain this space. Other proposed models include an iterative split-merge algorithm BIBREF18 and a graph-partitioning based approach BIBREF1 . marquez2008semantic provide a good overview of the supervised SRL systems.
